name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
title: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
answer: Weighing the scientific consensus is the practice of judging how much agreement exists in a body of research on a given question. It goes beyond counting papers to consider study quality, consistency of results, and the strength of the underlying evidence. This work sits inside literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is to distinguish a robust consensus from a contested or premature one. It also involves recognising when a consensus is shifting or when a field lacks enough evidence to support any firm conclusion.

sections.body: Weighing the scientific consensus is the practice of judging how much agreement exists in a body of research on a given question. It goes beyond counting papers to consider study quality, consistency of results, and the strength of the underlying evidence. This work sits inside literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is to distinguish a robust consensus from a contested or premature one. It also involves recognising when a consensus is shifting or when a field lacks enough evidence to support any firm conclusion.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on literature databases, reference managers, and systematic review software for screening and data extraction. Text mining and claim extraction tools help map findings across large corpora. This site's library holds 135 research papers and 12026 claims extracted from research works, which can be analysed to see where studies agree or conflict. The site also catalogues 800 scientific models and 732 AI tools, some of which support automated screening, data extraction, and evidence mapping.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with a focused question and a search strategy that aims to capture all relevant studies. Reviewers screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, and extract data on methods, results, and risk of bias. Synthesis often uses meta-analysis to pool effect sizes, with tests for heterogeneity and publication bias. For consensus specifically, reviewers may also use qualitative methods such as Delphi panels or framework synthesis to weigh expert agreement alongside statistical evidence.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area centre on attribution, reproducibility, and the honest representation of disagreement. Every claim should be traceable to its original paper, and this site never links to the Consensus search tool, it links to the original paper. Reviewers must manage conflicts of interest and avoid cherry-picking studies that support a preferred conclusion. Risks include overstating consensus when evidence is thin, and understating it when a field is genuinely settled. Provenance matters because a consensus claim is only as good as the studies behind it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward living systematic reviews that update as new evidence appears. Automated claim extraction and network analysis are making it easier to track agreement across thousands of papers. AI tools are increasingly used to assist screening and data extraction, though human judgement remains central to weighing consensus. The main challenge ahead is to keep consensus assessments transparent and timely, especially when public debate demands quick answers on contested topics.
